Reviewer capacity covers only a third of the findings the pass produces, and today reviewers pick findings to check in arbitrary order. How should the verification pass be changed so that limited review attention lands on the right findings?
options: Have the pass self-report confidence alongside each finding and calibrate routing thresholds against review outcomes, sending low-confidence findings to humans first
Route findings to reviewers in descending severity order, since critical findings are the ones where a verification mistake costs most
Have reviewers check the first third of findings in each run's output order, keeping the routing rule simple and auditable
Suppress the findings the verification pass seems least certain about so the remaining volume matches reviewer capacity
optionExplanations: Correct. The pattern is verification passes that self-report confidence alongside each finding to enable calibrated review routing — the scores are made trustworthy by calibrating thresholds against actual review outcomes, and scarce reviewer attention concentrates where verification is least certain.

Tempting because severity reflects stakes, but it measures impact if true, not likelihood of being wrong — a confidently verified critical finding needs less human checking than a shaky medium one, so severity-only routing spends attention on the wrong axis.

Tempting because it is simple and reproducible, but output order carries no information about which findings deserve scrutiny — the sample is arbitrary, so the same reviewer capacity catches strictly fewer verification errors than informed routing would.

Tempting because it fits volume to capacity, but silently suppressing uncertain findings inverts the logic: the least-certain findings are exactly the ones that need human eyes, and uncalibrated suppression discards them with no outcome data ever collected.
principle: self-reported confidence, calibrated on outcomes, routes review attention
relatedConcept: Verification passes emit per-finding confidence; calibration against review outcomes makes the routing trustworthy.
overallExplanation: Have the pass emit per-finding confidence and calibrate routing thresholds on review outcomes. Severity ranks impact rather than doubt, arbitrary sampling wastes capacity, and suppression hides what most needs checking.

objective: Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
question: A CI pipeline has Claude Code implement a fix for each incoming ticket and then, in the same session, runs a 'review the change you just made' step before opening the pull request. Post-merge defect rates are no lower than before the review step was added. What change to the pipeline is most likely to make the automated review effective?
options: Run the review as a separate independent Claude instance that receives the diff without the implementing session's conversation and reasoning
Include the prior review's findings in the same session and instruct it to report only new or still-unaddressed issues on each iteration
Instruct the same session to review the diff as if it had been written by another developer it has never worked with
Add a second same-session review round after the first, so the change is examined twice before the pull request opens
optionExplanations: Correct. A session that generated code retains the reasoning behind its decisions and is unlikely to question them — which is why the review step adds nothing. An independent instance receives only the diff, evaluates it without the generator's rationalizations, and catches what self-review approves.

Tempting because that is a real CI practice, but it solves a different problem — duplicate comments across re-reviews after new commits. It does nothing about the core defect here: the reviewing session still carries the reasoning context that produced the change.

Tempting because reframing sounds like fresh eyes, but the pretense does not remove the context — the session still holds the actual reasoning that justified every decision, and role-play instructions cannot make it forget why it believed the code was correct.

Tempting because two examinations feel more thorough, but both rounds run inside the same context with the same commitments — a second agreement from the same biased reviewer is not additional scrutiny, just additional cost and latency.
principle: independent review instances, not self-review steps, catch generator blind spots
relatedConcept: Session context isolation in CI: the session that wrote the change is the wrong session to review it.
overallExplanation: Route the diff to an independent instance without the implementing session's context. Self-review — however instructed, repeated, or role-played — inherits the reasoning that produced the defects.

objective: Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
question: A platform team uses Claude to generate framework-migration pull requests touching 30+ files each, then needs automated review before humans look. Early attempts — asking the generating session to double-check itself, and reviewing all 30 files in one pass — missed cross-file breakages and produced contradictory per-file verdicts. Which two architectural choices fix this? (Choose two.)
options: Review with an independent Claude instance that has no access to the generating session's reasoning context
Split the review into per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow
Keep the review in the generating session but enable extended thinking so it deliberates longer over each file
Run the single whole-PR pass three times and post only the findings that appear in a majority of the runs
optionExplanations: Correct. The generating session retains the reasoning that produced the migration and will not challenge its own decisions; an independent instance without that context evaluates the changes on their merits — the fix for self-review consistently blessing its own output.

Correct. Thirty files in one pass dilutes attention, producing exactly the observed symptoms: contradictory verdicts on the same pattern and missed cross-file breakage. Per-file passes give each file consistent depth, and a dedicated integration pass examines the data flow between them.

Tempting because longer deliberation sounds like deeper review, but extended thinking extends reasoning that begins inside the generator's own context — more careful thought within the same blind spot, which independent instances are specifically noted to outperform.

Tempting because majority voting filters unstable output, but each run suffers the same attention dilution over 30 files, and agreement measures repeatability rather than correctness — intermittently caught real defects are voted out while stable misjudgments survive.
principle: isolate the reviewer and split the pass: independence plus multi-pass
relatedConcept: Large generated changesets need both context isolation (separate instance) and attention management (per-file + integration passes).
overallExplanation: Combine an independent review instance with per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass. Extended thinking and majority voting leave both root causes — generator context and attention dilution — untouched.

objective: Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
question: An automated reviewer analyzes each file of a pull request in its own focused pass, and per-file feedback quality is consistently strong. Last week it approved a PR in which one file changed a date field's serialization format while a consumer in another file still parsed the old format — a production incident followed. What should be added to the architecture?
options: A separate integration pass that examines cross-file data flow across the full changeset after the per-file passes complete
An expansion of each per-file pass's input to include the full contents of every other changed file for reference
A rule that per-file passes flag any change to serialization logic for mandatory human review before merge
A second round of per-file passes with a different prompt emphasis, so each file is examined twice before approval
optionExplanations: Correct. Per-file passes are scoped to local issues by design — a producer-consumer mismatch is invisible when each file is judged alone. The multi-pass architecture pairs them with a cross-file integration pass that analyzes data flow across the changeset, which is exactly what this defect required.

Tempting because full visibility would technically expose the mismatch, but loading every other file into every per-file pass recreates the attention-diluted single-pass review the per-file design exists to avoid — analysis quality degrades across the board.

Tempting because it would have caught this incident, but it is a patch for one defect signature: the next cross-file breakage will involve an enum, a route, or a config key, not serialization. The architectural gap is the missing integration pass, not a missing keyword rule.

Tempting because a second emphasis catches more local issues, but both rounds still judge each file in isolation — no number of per-file passes, under any prompt, can see a contract broken between two files that are never examined together.
principle: per-file passes catch local issues; only an integration pass sees cross-file contracts
relatedConcept: Multi-pass review = focused per-file analysis plus a dedicated cross-file data-flow pass; each covers what the other cannot.
overallExplanation: Add a cross-file integration pass after the per-file passes. Producer-consumer mismatches live between files, where isolated per-file review — however thorough or repeated — cannot look.
